definition.text: A factor that corrects a substance's concentration for how far a mixture departs from ideal behaviour.

facts.text: Activity equals the activity coefficient times concentration; in an ideal electrolyte solution all coefficients equal one, which only very dilute solutions approach.
Activity coefficients matter especially in soil chemistry, where small volumes of water hold high concentrations of electrolytes.
Coefficients change with concentration because ions interact more as the electrolyte becomes more concentrated.
Cation and anion coefficients cannot be measured separately, so a mean activity coefficient, γ±, is used.
pH is defined from hydrogen ion activity, a definition IUPAC calls only notional because single-ion activities cannot be measured.
They can be calculated with the Debye–Hückel equation or extensions such as the Davies and Pitzer equations, or specific ion interaction theory.
For uncharged species such as dissolved CO2 the coefficient follows a salting-out model, log10 γ = bI, with b for CO2 0.11 at 10 °C.

definition.text: A measure of the concentration of ions in a solution, weighted by their charge.

facts.text: Molar ionic strength is I = ½ Σ ci zi², summed over every ion, where c is molar concentration and z the ion's charge number.
For NaCl the ionic strength equals the concentration, but MgSO4, with doubly charged ions, gives four times as much; multivalent ions contribute strongly.
It can be molar or molal, so units should be stated; molality is preferred for non-ideal solutions.
Total electrolyte concentration affects dissociation constants and the solubility of salts.
The Debye length, which characterizes double-layer thickness, is inversely proportional to the square root of ionic strength; more or higher-valence counterions compress the double layer.
It plays a central role in Debye–Hückel theory of non-ideal ionic solutions.
Lewis and Randall introduced the concept in 1921 when describing activity coefficients of strong electrolytes.

definition.text: A theory by Peter Debye and Erich Hückel explaining why electrolyte solutions depart from ideal behaviour.

facts.text: A linearized Poisson–Boltzmann model, it predicts mean ionic activity coefficients accurately in dilute solution and underlies modern treatments.
Non-ideality arises mainly because unlike ions attract and like ions repel, so ions are not randomly distributed.
Each ion is pictured surrounded by a statistically averaged cloud of net opposite charge.
It assumes complete dissociation, spherical unpolarized ions and a solvent acting only as a medium of constant permittivity.
Its limiting law makes the logarithm of the mean activity coefficient proportional to the square root of ionic strength.
It fits measurements below about 10⁻³ mol/L, deviating at higher concentrations and with more highly charged ions.
The extended equation is accurate up to ionic strength 0.1; beyond that the Pitzer equations should be used.
Debye and Hückel published it in 1923 in Physikalische Zeitschrift.

definition.text: The carrying down by a precipitate of substances that would normally stay dissolved under the same conditions.

facts.text: It works by inclusion in the crystal lattice, occlusion of adsorbed impurities trapped as the crystal grows, or adsorption onto the precipitate's surface.
Trace elements too dilute to precipitate alone are coprecipitated with a carrier of similar crystal structure.
It matters in acid mine drainage, radionuclide migration around waste repositories, heavy metal transport and wastewater treatment.
Constructed wetlands remove phosphorus by coprecipitation with iron, aluminium and calcium compounds, and iron coagulants remove arsenic from water the same way.

definition.text: An empirical adsorption isotherm relating the amount adsorbed on a solid to the gas pressure or solute concentration.

facts.text: It is written x/m = K c^(1/n), where x/m is adsorbate mass per adsorbent mass and K and n are constants for a given pair at a given temperature.
In log form, log x/m = log K + (1/n) log c, a straight line.
Freundlich fitted it to adsorption of organic acids on coal from water.
Being empirical, it should give way to theoretically based isotherms such as Langmuir or BET when those fit.
It can also be derived from surface heterogeneity: high-energy sites fill first, then low-energy ones, so the heat of adsorption weakens with coverage.
A good fit makes a heterogeneous surface only likely, not proved; calorimetry can confirm it.
It fails at high pressure, where adsorption saturates.

conflicts.text: The first mathematical fit to an isotherm was published by Freundlich and Kuster in 1906.
conflicts.note: The Freundlich equation page dates Freundlich's expression to 1909 (S:c82536c45321) and his numerical work to 1907 (S:93f36f1632fc).

definition.text: A model of adsorption on a surface of identical sites, each holding at most one adsorbate molecule, with adsorption and desorption reversible.

facts.text: Binding is treated as a reaction between an adsorbate molecule and an empty site, with an equilibrium constant.
The isotherm is θ = K p / (1 + K p), where θ is the fraction of sites occupied.
At low pressure θ is about Kp; at high pressure θ approaches 1.
It assumes a flat homogeneous surface, immobile adsorbate, equal adsorption energy at every site, monolayer coverage and no interactions between adsorbed molecules.
It deviates in many cases because it ignores surface roughness, with its several site types, and interactions between adsorbates.
Its competitive form lets two species compete for the same sites, each site holding one or the other.
It nonetheless remains the first choice for most adsorption models.
Irving Langmuir presented it in 1916 and won the 1932 Nobel Prize for his surface chemistry.

conflicts.text: Irving Langmuir derived the first scientifically based adsorption isotherm in 1918.
conflicts.note: The Langmuir adsorption model page gives 1916 (S:404a89926886).

definition.text: Using chemical thermodynamics, kinetics or both, usually by computer, to analyse the chemical reactions in geological systems, including low-temperature aqueous solutions near the Earth's surface.

facts.text: Models are built to understand natural water composition, contaminant mobility in groundwater and the ion speciation of plant nutrients in soil.
Garrels and Thompson first applied it in 1962, by hand, as an equilibrium model predicting species distributions, mineral saturation states and gas fugacities from bulk solution composition.
Coupling mass transfer to an equilibrium model gives a reaction path model; Helgeson's 1968 program first solved these, modelling processes such as weathering.
A model starts from a basis of aqueous species, minerals and gases, as many as the system's components, then solves mass action and mass balance equations for equilibrium.
A mineral's saturation index (log Q/K) is zero at equilibrium, positive when supersaturated and likely to precipitate, and negative when it tends to dissolve.
Reactions simulated include acid–base, aqueous complexation, dissolution and precipitation, redox, and sorption, ion exchange and surface complexation.
Coupling with hydrologic transport models gives reactive transport models of reactions along a flowpath.
Differences between thermodynamic databases can cause large uncertainties, which are seldom considered.

definition.text: A surface complex in which an ion binds directly to a mineral surface with no water molecules between them.

facts.text: Only ions with a high affinity for surface sites form them, including specifically adsorbed ions that bond covalently.
In outer sphere complexes water separates the ion from the surface; in inner sphere ones surface hydroxyl groups act as σ-donor ligands.
On oxide surfaces the metal ion acts as a Lewis acid and the ligand as a Lewis base; sorption of protonated ligands depends on pH.
They govern the transport and retention of trace elements in soil, where natural sorbents are often metal oxides.
Oxyanions such as sulfate can hinder the dissolution of iron and manganese oxides, slowing or preventing reductive dissolution.
Alkaline earth metals sorb less as their ion size increases, so they become more mobile during weathering.
In birnessite, cations such as Ca, Cu, Zn, Pb and Cd form inner-sphere complexes above and below vacancies in the oxide layers.
Through these interactions soil properties influence how nutrients and pollutants are retained or depleted.

definition.text: The ratio of a compound's concentrations in two immiscible phases at equilibrium.

facts.text: Strictly, the partition coefficient covers only the un-ionized form, while the distribution coefficient covers all forms of the compound.
With water and a hydrophobic solvent such as octanol, it measures how hydrophilic or hydrophobic a substance is.
Hydrogeologists use the octanol–water coefficient Kow to predict how dissolved hydrophobic organic compounds migrate in soil and groundwater.
Partition coefficients can also be defined when one or both phases are solid.

definition.text: Detailed structure in X-ray absorption spectra whose analysis reveals an atom's local structure and unoccupied electronic states.

facts.text: Spectra divide into the edge region, the XANES region spanning 50–100 eV around the threshold, and the EXAFS region; XAFS denotes XANES plus EXAFS.
EXAFS, from single scattering of the photoelectron by neighbouring atoms, gives local structure; XANES multiple-scattering peaks give its geometry.
Surface EXAFS reveals the coordination structure and chemical state of adsorbates.
XANES and EXAFS, with X-ray diffraction, are used to evaluate how microbes sorb and mineralize radionuclides in bioremediation.

definition.text: A calculation of the concentrations of all the chemical species present in a solution.

facts.text: Geochemical equilibrium models predict species distributions from measurements of bulk solution composition.
Such models are used to work out the ion speciation of plant nutrients in soil and of regulated metals in stored wastes.
Trace metals form complexes with hydroxide, carbonate and chloride, and their speciation changes between oxidized and reduced conditions.
Element toxicity varies with oxidation state, so food regulations require speciation of some elements.
